statement: In a two-way collateral agreement, whichever party has a negative mark-to-market value on the portfolio posts collateral to the other, so the direction of posting can change as exposure changes.
explanation: Two-way means either party may be the collateral provider, depending on which side of the net exposure it is on. If the portfolio value changes sign, the collateral flows reverse.
originalText: Whichever party has a negative mark‑to‑market value on the portfolio posts collateral to the other, so the direction of posting can change as exposure changes.

statement: In a two-way collateral agreement, both parties must post collateral at all times, regardless of the sign of the mark-to-market value.
explanation: Collateral covers only the net exposure of the receiving party. A party that is in-the-money on the portfolio is not required to post.
originalText: Both parties must post collateral at all times, regardless of the sign of the mark‑to‑market value.

statement: In a two-way collateral agreement, only the party with the weaker credit rating ever posts collateral and the other party never does.
explanation: That describes a one-way agreement, in which only one party ever posts. In a two-way agreement either party may post, depending on the sign of the net exposure.
originalText: Only the party with the weaker credit rating ever posts collateral, and the other party never does.

statement: Either party to a collateral agreement may unilaterally change the collateral terms at any time if its counterparty's credit quality deteriorates.
explanation: Collateral terms can be linked to credit quality only through pre-agreed provisions such as rating triggers. A signed agreement cannot be amended unilaterally.
originalText: Either party may unilaterally change the collateral terms at any time if its counterparty’s credit quality deteriorates.

statement: A tiered threshold approach, in which thresholds are linked to counterparty credit ratings and lower-rated counterparties have lower thresholds, balances risk management with operational efficiency.
explanation: The threshold is the exposure left uncollateralised, so it should reflect credit quality. Rating-linked thresholds minimise workload for strong counterparties while protecting against weak ones.
originalText: The bank decides to adopt a tiered threshold approach, where threshold levels are linked to the credit ratings of counterparties, with lower‑rated counterparties having lower thresholds.

statement: Under a one-way CSA, the party that does not post collateral is likely to pay charges for the counterparty risk (CVA), funding (FVA), collateral terms (ColVA) and/or capital requirements (KVA) that it imposes on the other party.
explanation: In a one-way CSA only one party posts, so the poster bears additional risk and costs. The non-posting party is expected to compensate it for the xVA it imposes.
originalText: If they agree to a one‑way CSA, the non‑collateral posting party is likely to pay charges for the counterparty risk (CVA), funding (FVA), collateral terms (ColVA), and/or capital requirements (KVA) they impose on the other party

statement: Credit support annexes are rare among derivative counterparties, so the most likely approach is that there is no CSA.
explanation: CSAs are not rare: banks almost always trade under CSAs and other financial institutions often do.
originalText: As CSAs are rare, the most likely approach is ”No CSA”

statement: A one-way CSA by definition specifies a threshold of zero.
explanation: In a one-way CSA the party that does not post effectively has an infinite threshold, because it never posts. Zero thresholds are typical of two-way interbank CSAs.
originalText: If they agree to a one‑way CSA, then by definition, the CSA will specify a threshold of zero

statement: Under a two-way CSA, either party can unilaterally edit the CSA after it has been signed.
explanation: A signed CSA is a contract and cannot be changed unilaterally. Amendments require the agreement of both parties.
originalText: If they agree to a two‑way CSA, then either party can unilaterally edit the CSA subsequent to signing the CSA

statement: When dealing with a hedge fund, a bank would most likely negotiate a one-way collateral agreement in the bank's favour, given the bank's stronger credit rating.
explanation: One-way agreements are used when counterparties differ significantly in credit quality, size or risk. A bank is typically of much higher credit quality than a hedge fund, so only the hedge fund posts collateral.
originalText: one‑way agreement in the bank’s favor given the bank’s stronger credit rating.

statement: When dealing with a hedge fund, a bank would most likely negotiate a two-way collateral agreement because of the small difference in credit quality between the two.
explanation: Two-way agreements suit similar counterparties such as banks. A bank and a hedge fund have a large, not small, credit quality gap, which supports a one-way agreement.
originalText: two‑way agreement given the relatively small difference in credit quality between the two entities.

statement: Collateralization of derivatives increases funding liquidity risk because collateral must be delivered on time, often within tight timescales.
explanation: Collateral calls require liquid assets within short timescales, so counterparty risk is partly transformed into funding liquidity risk.
originalText: It increases funding liquidity risk due to the need for timely payments, often within tight timescales.

statement: Collateralization of derivatives reduces operational risk by simplifying trade entry and settlement processes.
explanation: Collateral management adds missed calls, failed deliveries and human error, so operational risk increases rather than decreases.
originalText: It reduces operational risk by simplifying trade entry and settlement processes.

statement: Collateralization of derivatives eliminates market risk by ensuring an objective valuation of the underlying transactions.
explanation: Residual market risk remains over the margin period of risk and within thresholds and minimum transfer amounts, so it is not eliminated.
originalText: It eliminates market risk by ensuring an objective valuation of the underlying transactions.

statement: Adding a bilateral collateral arrangement to a derivatives contract that previously had no collateral reduces counterparty risk.
explanation: Collateral lowers exposure to the counterparty's default. It transforms risk into operational, market and funding liquidity risks rather than removing it.
originalText: Acme reduced counterparty risk

statement: Adding a bilateral collateral arrangement to a derivatives contract reduces operational risk.
explanation: Operational risk rises, because collateral handling creates more processes (calls, valuation, delivery, reconciliation) and more chances for error.
originalText: Acme reduced operational risk

statement: Inaccurate valuation of collateral, leading to inadequate collateral postings and disputes with counterparties, is an example of operational risk arising from collateralization.
explanation: Operational risk from collateral comes from handling: valuation errors, missed calls, failed deliveries and computer or human error. Wrong valuations cause wrong call amounts and disputes.
originalText: Operational risk emerges due to inaccurate valuation of collateral, leading to inadequate collateral postings and potential disputes with counterparties.

statement: Using diversified collateral mitigates operational risk by reducing exposure to any single asset's volatility.
explanation: Diversification addresses market and concentration risk of the collateral, not process failures, which are what operational risk covers.
originalText: Operational risk is mitigated through the use of diversified collateral, reducing the bank’s exposure to any single asset’s volatility.

statement: Operational risk is unaffected by collateralization practices, because it is concerned mainly with market fluctuations and credit risk management.
explanation: Collateralization adds operational risk through missed calls, failed deliveries and errors. Operational risk concerns processes, people and systems, not market or credit risk.
originalText: Operational risk is unaffected by collateralization practices, as it is primarily concerned with market fluctuations and credit risk management.

statement: A firm faces funding liquidity risk in collateralization when it must post additional high-quality liquid assets as collateral during market downturns, potentially leading to a liquidity shortfall.
explanation: Margin calls rise in stress, just when liquid assets are hardest and most expensive to obtain, so calls can exceed available liquid assets.
originalText: GFB faces funding liquidity risk when it has to post additional high‑quality liquid assets as collateral during market downturns, potentially leading to a liquidity shortfall.

statement: Using long-term, illiquid assets as collateral minimises funding liquidity risk by securing a firm's obligations for an extended period.
explanation: Posting illiquid assets does not reduce liquidity risk. Eligible collateral is typically cash or high-quality securities, and illiquid assets worsen liquidity strain.
originalText: The use of long‑term, illiquid assets as collateral by GFB minimizes funding liquidity risk by securing its obligations for an extended period.

statement: Market moves between the last collateral posting and the receipt of collateral after a default can leave exposure only partly covered, so some residual market risk remains under collateralization.
explanation: Collateral is called and delivered only periodically, subject to the threshold and minimum transfer amount. Over the margin period of risk exposure can grow uncollateralised.
originalText: Market moves between the last collateral posting and the receipt of collateral after default can leave exposure only partly covered, so some residual risk remains.

statement: Posting collateral eliminates all market risk because exposure is reset to zero at every valuation date.
explanation: Exposure is not reset to zero continuously. The delay (margin period of risk), the threshold and the minimum transfer amount all leave residual market risk.
originalText: Posting collateral eliminates all market risk because exposure is reset to zero at every valuation date.

statement: Market risk in a collateralised derivatives agreement arises only when the collateral is cash held in a different currency from the trade.
explanation: A currency mismatch is one source of FX risk, but the market risk created by collateralization comes mainly from exposure moving over the margin period of risk and within thresholds and minimum transfer amounts.
originalText: Market risk arises only when the collateral is cash held in a different currency from the trade.

statement: A bank that hedges uncollateralised client transactions with bilaterally collateralised trades faces an imbalance in collateral flows, because it must fund margin on the hedge without receiving offsetting margin on the client trade.
explanation: When the client trade moves in the client's favour, the bank posts margin on the hedge but receives none on the client trade. This one-sided margin flow strains liquidity.
originalText: Discrepancy between uncollateralized client transactions and bilaterally collateralized hedges.

statement: A company that pays fixed on a collateralised swap hedging its floating-rate debt faces funding liquidity risk when rates fall, because it must post variation margin immediately while the benefit of lower interest on its debt arrives only gradually.
explanation: When rates fall the swap's mark-to-market turns negative for the fixed payer, who must deliver variation margin daily. The debt savings accrue slowly as coupons reset.
originalText: Funding liquidity risk, because the swap has a negative MtM and Global must post liquid variation margin immediately, while the offsetting benefit (lower interest on its debt) arrives only gradually.

statement: Daily exchange of variation margin reduces operational risk by automatically eliminating valuation disputes and failed deliveries.
explanation: Daily margining increases the operational burden (calls, delivery, valuation, reconciliation) and the chance of disputes and failures, rather than reducing them.
originalText: Reduced operational risk, because daily margin automatically eliminates valuation disputes and failed deliveries.

statement: Minimum transfer amounts, thresholds and the margin period of risk leave exposure that can move before collateral is received, creating market risk.
explanation: Between the last posting and the receipt of collateral, market moves can increase exposure. This residual, hard-to-hedge risk is market risk created by collateralization.
originalText: Minimum transfer amounts, thresholds and the margin period of risk leave exposure that can move before collateral is received, creating market risk.

statement: Missed collateral calls, failed deliveries and human error create market risk.
explanation: Process failures such as missed calls, failed deliveries and human error are operational risk, not market risk.
originalText: Missed collateral calls, failed deliveries and human error create market risk.

statement: Price impact and transaction costs incurred when liquidating a large collateral position create operational risk.
explanation: Price impact and liquidation costs are liquidity (liquidation) risk, not operational risk.
originalText: Price impact and transaction costs when liquidating a large collateral position create operational risk.

statement: Difficulty in meeting frequent, large margin calls creates operational risk.
explanation: The inability to fund margin calls is funding liquidity risk. Operational risk concerns errors and failures in processes.
originalText: Difficulty in meeting frequent, large margin calls creates operational risk.

statement: Liquidation risk occurs when the amount of a security sold is large relative to its typical trading volume, which may drive down its price.
explanation: Selling an amount large relative to normal volume can move the price and cause a substantial loss. Selling slowly instead exposes the holder to market volatility during liquidation.
originalText: Liquidation risk occurs when the amount of a security sold is large relative to its typical trading volume, which may drive down its price.

statement: Liquidity risk in collateral agreements is eliminated entirely once an appropriate haircut is applied to the collateral.
explanation: A haircut gives a buffer but does not remove price-impact losses that exceed the haircut.
originalText: Liquidity risk is eliminated entirely once an appropriate haircut is applied to the collateral.

statement: Liquidation risk arises only if the issuer of the collateral security defaults, not from the size of the position sold.
explanation: Issuer default is a separate risk. Liquidation risk is driven mainly by the size of the sale relative to market depth.
originalText: Liquidation risk arises only if the issuer of the collateral security defaults, not from the size of the position sold.

statement: Liquidity risk occurs when there are potential pitfalls in the handling of collateral, including human error.
explanation: Pitfalls in handling collateral, including human error, are operational risk. Liquidity risk concerns funding margin calls and the cost of selling assets.
originalText: Liquidity risk occurs when there are potential pitfalls in the handling of collateral, including human error.

statement: A shorter remargining period decreases exposure to market volatility, because collateral is adjusted more frequently and the period during which exposure can rise uncollateralised is smaller.
explanation: The margin period of risk creates exposure equal to the change in value that can occur before collateral is received. Shortening it reduces that change.
originalText: It decreases exposure to market volatility because collateral is adjusted more frequently, shrinking the period during which exposure can rise uncollateralized.

statement: A shorter remargining period increases exposure to market volatility and counterparty risk.
explanation: The relationship is reversed: a longer, not shorter, remargining period gives exposure more time to grow before collateral arrives.
originalText: It increases exposure to market volatility and counterparty risk.
correction: A longer remargining period increases exposure to market volatility and counterparty risk.

statement: The length of the remargining period has no significant impact on credit exposure.
explanation: The margin period of risk is a primary driver of residual exposure under collateralization, especially in volatile markets.
originalText: It has no significant impact on exposure.

statement: Lowering the threshold in a collateral agreement reduces credit risk, because collateral is called for smaller exposures.
explanation: The threshold is exposure left uncollateralised by design, so the lower it is, the less exposure remains uncovered.
originalText: Lowering the threshold reduces credit risk because collateral is called for smaller exposures.

statement: Increasing the threshold in a collateral agreement reduces credit risk because more collateral is posted.
explanation: A higher threshold means less collateral is called, so more exposure stays uncollateralised and credit risk increases.
originalText: Increasing the threshold reduces credit risk because more collateral is posted.
correction: Increasing the threshold in a collateral agreement increases credit risk because less collateral is posted.

statement: The threshold in a collateral agreement has no significant impact on credit risk and only affects operational efficiency.
explanation: The threshold directly determines the amount of exposure that is never collateralised, so it matters for credit risk as well as for operations.
originalText: The threshold has no significant impact on credit risk; it only affects operational efficiency.

statement: A higher threshold in a collateral agreement reduces credit risk because it lowers the frequency of collateral calls.
explanation: A higher threshold does reduce call frequency and administrative cost, but it increases, not decreases, credit risk because more exposure is uncollateralised.
originalText: A higher threshold reduces credit risk because it lowers the frequency of collateral calls.
correction: A higher threshold in a collateral agreement increases credit risk even though it lowers the frequency of collateral calls.

changes.from: reduces credit risk because it lowers
changes.to: increases credit risk even though it lowers

statement: For risk assessment, the remargin period equals the legal margin call frequency, which is typically one day.
explanation: The margin period of risk runs from the call to actual receipt and includes valuation, delivery, settlement and legal delays on top of the call frequency, so it is longer than the margin call frequency.
originalText: For risk assessment, the remargin period will equal the legal margin call frequency, i.e. typically one day.

statement: If a position is strongly collateralized, the primary concerns are the length of the remargin period and the volatilities of the exposure and the collateral.
explanation: With zero threshold and no initial margin, the residual risk comes from the margin period of risk and from the volatility of the exposure and of the collateral.
originalText: If a position is strongly collateralized, the primary concerns are the length of the remargin period and the volatilities of the exposure and the collateral.

statement: Imperfect collateralization at a given date can arise from the terms of the collateral agreement (threshold, minimum transfer amount, rounding), which prevent the full amount from being called.
explanation: Thresholds, minimum transfer amounts and rounding all prevent the full exposure from being called.
originalText: Imperfect collateralization at a given date can arise from the terms of the collateral agreement (threshold, minimum transfer amount, rounding), which prevent calling the full amount.

statement: Exposure may increase between margin calls, and that portion of the exposure cannot be collateralized.
explanation: Collateral is called only at discrete dates, so any exposure growth between calls remains uncollateralised until the next call and delivery.
originalText: Exposure may increase between margin calls, and that portion cannot be collateralized.

statement: A lower collateral threshold implies that a larger portion of exposure is protected by collateral.
explanation: The threshold is an amount of exposure that is never collateralised, so reducing it increases the share of exposure covered by collateral.
originalText: A lower threshold implies that a larger portion of exposure is protected by collateral.

statement: A shorter margin period of risk implies that a smaller portion of exposure is protected by collateral.
explanation: A shorter margin period of risk leaves less time for exposure to grow before collateral arrives, so more of the exposure is protected.
originalText: A shorter margin period of risk implies that a smaller portion of exposure is protected by collateral.
correction: A shorter margin period of risk implies that a larger portion of exposure is protected by collateral.

statement: A lower independent amount (initial margin) implies that a larger portion of exposure is protected by collateral.
explanation: Lower initial margin means a smaller collateral cushion, so a smaller portion of exposure is protected.
originalText: A lower independent amount (initial margin) implies that a larger portion of exposure is protected by collateral.
correction: A lower independent amount (initial margin) implies that a smaller portion of exposure is protected by collateral.

statement: The protection from collateral specified in a CSA is uniform throughout the life of the exposure profile.
explanation: Collateral is path-dependent, and the threshold and minimum transfer amount bind differently as exposure changes, so protection is not uniform over time.
originalText: The protection from collateral specified in the CSA is uniform throughout the life of the exposure profile.

statement: A higher collateral threshold reduces the frequency of collateral exchanges and administrative cost but increases uncollateralised credit risk.
explanation: A higher threshold means collateral is only called for exposure above it, so there are fewer calls but a larger permanently uncollateralised amount.
originalText: A higher threshold reduces the frequency of collateral exchanges and administrative cost but increases uncollateralized credit risk.

statement: A longer remargining period reduces both operational burden and exposure to market value changes of the derivatives.
explanation: A longer remargining period lengthens the margin period of risk and so increases exposure; the operational saving does not offset this.
originalText: A longer remargining period reduces both operational burden and exposure to market value changes of the derivatives.
correction: A longer remargining period reduces operational burden but increases exposure to market value changes of the derivatives.

changes.from: reduces both operational burden and exposure
changes.to: reduces operational burden but increases exposure

statement: A lower minimum transfer amount increases the frequency of collateral movements, which reduces both exposure and transaction costs.
explanation: More frequent collateral movements reduce exposure but raise operational and transaction costs.
originalText: A lower minimum transfer amount increases the frequency of collateral movements, which reduces both exposure and transaction costs.
correction: A lower minimum transfer amount increases the frequency of collateral movements, which reduces exposure but increases transaction costs.

changes.from: reduces both exposure and transaction costs
changes.to: reduces exposure but increases transaction costs

statement: Shortening the remargining period and lowering the threshold and minimum transfer amount have no significant impact on exposure.
explanation: The threshold, minimum transfer amount and margin period of risk are the main sources of residual exposure under collateralization, so changing them matters.
originalText: Shortening the remargining period and lowering the threshold and minimum transfer amount have no significant impact on exposure.

statement: A larger independent amount (initial margin) posted by the counterparty increases the risk of a collateralised expected exposure profile.
explanation: Initial margin held acts as a cushion against exposure and therefore reduces expected exposure, whereas the other terms each leave exposure uncollateralised.
originalText: A larger independent amount (initial margin) posted by the counterparty
correction: A larger independent amount (initial margin) posted by the counterparty reduces the risk of a collateralised expected exposure profile.

statement: A longer remargin period tends to increase the risk of the expected exposure profile of a collateralised position.
explanation: A longer margin period of risk means exposure can grow for longer before collateral is received.
originalText: A longer remargin period

statement: A higher collateral threshold tends to increase the risk of the expected exposure profile of a collateralised position.
explanation: The threshold is exposure that is never collateralised, so a higher threshold leaves more exposure uncovered.
originalText: A higher threshold

statement: A larger minimum transfer amount tends to increase the risk of the expected exposure profile of a collateralised position.
explanation: Exposure below the minimum transfer amount is not called, so a larger minimum transfer amount means a larger uncollateralised gap.
originalText: A larger minimum transfer amount

statement: The annual review and renegotiation of the collateral threshold in the credit support annex is one of the time steps that make up the margin period of risk.
explanation: The margin period of risk measures only the operational and legal delays between the margin call and the completed close-out and re-hedge. A periodic review of the threshold is not part of that chain.
originalText: Annual review and renegotiation of the collateral threshold in the credit support annex

statement: The margin period of risk includes the time needed to value the exposure and collateral and to make the margin call.
explanation: Valuation of exposure and collateral and issuing a valid margin call is the first time step of the margin period of risk.
originalText: Valuation of the exposure and collateral, and the margin call

statement: The margin period of risk includes the grace period allowed to the counterparty before it is deemed to have failed to pay.
explanation: The grace period before a failure to pay becomes a default is one of the time steps; excluding it would understate the margin period of risk.
originalText: Grace period allowed to the counterparty before it is deemed to have failed to pay

statement: The margin period of risk includes the time needed to settle the collateral that is delivered.
explanation: Settlement time (cash intraday, government bonds about one day, corporate bonds about three days) is one of the time steps of the margin period of risk.
originalText: Settlement of the collateral that is delivered

statement: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the default probability term is the conditional default probability, i.e. the probability of default in the interval given survival to $t_{j-1}$.
explanation: The default probability in the formula is the marginal (unconditional) probability that default occurs within the interval, measured from today.
originalText: The fourth component is the conditional default probability, i.e. the probability of default in the interval given survival to t(j‑1).
correction: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the default probability term is the marginal default probability, i.e. the probability of default in the interval as seen from today.

statement: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the loss given default term is one minus the expected recovery rate.
explanation: The first component is LGD, which equals 1 minus the recovery rate.
originalText: The first component is loss given default, i.e. one minus the expected recovery rate.

statement: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the discount factor is the risk-free discount factor for the relevant date.
explanation: Each expected loss is discounted using the risk-free discount factor $DF(t_j)$.
originalText: The second component is the risk‑free discount factor for date t(j).

statement: In the simplified CVA formula with no wrong-way risk, the exposure term is the expected exposure at the relevant future dates.
explanation: With no wrong-way risk, exposure and default are independent, so CVA uses the expected exposure profile EE$(t_j)$.
originalText: The third component is the expected exposure at the relevant future dates.

statement: Bilateral exposure recognises that when the counterparty defaults the institution is paid only a recovery fraction of its positive exposure, which is a loss, whereas when the institution defaults the counterparty receives only a recovery fraction of the negative exposure, which is a gain for the institution.
explanation: Bilateral counterparty risk assumes that both parties can default: the loss on positive exposure is the CVA side and the gain on negative exposure is the DVA side.
originalText: When the counterparty defaults, the institution is only paid a recovery fraction of their exposure which is a loss for the institution. On the other hand, when the institution defaults, the counterparty receives a recovery fraction of the negative exposure which is a gain for the institution.

statement: Bilateral exposure is the worst exposure an institution could have at a certain time in the future, measured at a specified level of confidence.
explanation: That describes potential future exposure (PFE), a high-percentile exposure measure. Bilateral exposure refers to both parties being able to default.
originalText: This is the worst exposure an institution could have at a certain time in the future measured at a specified level of confidence.

statement: If all market participants agree on the BCVA approach and parameters, the total counterparty risk in the market (the sum of all BCVAs) equals the sum of all expected exposures.
explanation: BCVA is symmetric: each party's adjustment is the exact opposite of its counterparty's, so BCVAs net to zero across the market in theory.
originalText: If all market participants agree on the BCVA approach and parameters, the total counterparty risk in the market (the sum of all BCVAs) equals the sum of all expected exposures.
correction: If all market participants agree on the BCVA approach and parameters, the total counterparty risk in the market (the sum of all BCVAs) is zero.

changes.from: equals the sum of all expected exposures

statement: The second term of bilateral CVA is the debt value adjustment (DVA), which corresponds to the institution defaulting first, when it books a gain if its mark-to-market is negative.
explanation: DVA is the gain the institution books because on its own default it would pay only a recovery on what it owes.
originalText: The second BCVA term is the debt value adjustment (DVA); it corresponds to the institution defaulting first, when it books a gain if its mark‑to‑market is negative.

statement: Unlike a unilateral CVA, which can only reduce the value of a position, BCVA can increase it when the DVA term outweighs the CVA term, so the risky value can exceed the risk-free value.
explanation: Unilateral CVA is always a cost, but DVA is a gain that can outweigh CVA, so the bilateral adjustment can be positive.
originalText: Unlike a unilateral CVA, which can only reduce the value of a position, BCVA can increase it when the DVA term outweighs the CVA term, so the risky value can exceed the risk‑free value.

statement: Netting does not always benefit an institution under BCVA; it can be a disadvantage when the DVA term dominates, which normally corresponds to the institution being riskier than its counterparty.
explanation: With netting, the DVA benefit from negative-MtM trades is partly lost. When DVA dominates, that loss can outweigh the CVA reduction.
originalText: Netting does not always benefit the institution under BCVA; it can be a disadvantage when the DVA term dominates, which normally corresponds to the institution being riskier than its counterparty.

statement: To value derivatives while reflecting both its own and its counterparties' credit risk, a firm applies debt value adjustment (DVA) together with CVA to obtain bilateral CVA (BCVA).
explanation: BCVA is CVA plus DVA, capturing both the counterparty's default and the firm's own default.
originalText: Implement DVA adjustments to reflect changes in the market’s perception of Acme’s credit risk, applying it in conjunction with CVA to determine BCVA for comprehensive valuation.

statement: Debt value adjustment (DVA) is no longer a recognised method for adjusting valuations for changes in a firm's own credit risk, so only CVA should be used.
explanation: DVA is recognised: accounting rules since FAS 157 and IFRS 13 require own credit risk to be reflected. Ignoring it reverts to a unilateral CVA.
originalText: Focus only on CVA because DVA is no longer a recognized method for adjusting valuations due to changes in the firm’s own credit risk.

statement: Debt value adjustment (DVA) has superseded CVA as the industry standard for incorporating credit risk in valuations.
explanation: DVA complements CVA rather than replacing it. Using DVA alone would ignore the counterparty's default.
originalText: Use DVA exclusively for valuation, considering that it has now superseded CVA as the industry standard for incorporating credit risk in valuations.

statement: Bilateral CVA should be calculated without the DVA term, because including a firm's own credit risk leads to double-counting in the valuation adjustments.
explanation: A BCVA without DVA is just a unilateral CVA. DVA is the mirror-image term for the institution's own default, not double counting.
originalText: Calculate BCVA as an extension of CVA but without including DVA, as including the firm’s own credit risk may lead to double‑counting in the valuation adjustments.

statement: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the institution has survived (not defaulted) up to time $t_{j-1}$.
explanation: A counterparty default only hurts the institution if the institution is still alive at that time, so the CVA term is conditioned on the institution's survival.
originalText: The probability that the Institution has survived (not defaulted) up to time $t_{j-1}$

statement: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the counterparty has survived up to time $t_{j-1}$.
explanation: The subscript I denotes the institution. The counterparty's default probability is already in PD$_C$, and its survival probability appears in the DVA term instead.
originalText: The probability that the Counterparty has survived up to time $t_{j-1}$
correction: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the institution has survived up to time $t_{j-1}$.

statement: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the institution has defaulted before time $t_{j-1}$.
explanation: $S_I$ is a survival probability. The probability of having defaulted is $1 - S_I$, and using it would reverse the first-to-default logic.
originalText: The probability that the Institution has defaulted before time $t_{j-1}$
correction: In Gregory's bilateral CVA formula, the factor $S_{I}(t_{j-1})$ that multiplies the CVA term is the probability that the institution has not defaulted before time $t_{j-1}$.

statement: Debt value adjustment (DVA) is the formalization of a term that incorporates specific wrong-way risk (dependence between exposure and counterparty default) into the CVA framework.
explanation: DVA is the bilateral complement to CVA for the institution's own default. Wrong-way risk is a separate dependence effect.
originalText: DVA is the formalization of a term that incorporates specific wrong‑way risk (i.e., dependence between exposure and counterparty default) in the CVA framework.

statement: Bilateral CVA is the sum of the credit value adjustment (CVA) and the debt value adjustment (DVA).
explanation: BCVA = CVA + DVA, with CVA a cost and DVA a gain.
originalText: Bilateral CVA is the sum of the credit value adjustment (CVA) and DVA.

statement: Compared with the risky value that includes only the unilateral CVA term, adding DVA increases the value of the risky position.
explanation: DVA is a gain that offsets part of the CVA cost, so the risky value is higher than under unilateral CVA alone.
originalText: Compared with the risky value that includes only the unilateral CVA term, adding DVA increases the value of the risky position.

statement: DVA is the mirror image of CVA: it is based on the expected negative exposure, the institution's own default probability and its loss given default.
explanation: DVA mirrors CVA's structure, replacing expected positive exposure and the counterparty's default probability with expected negative exposure and the institution's own default probability.
originalText: DVA is the mirror image of CVA: it is based on the expected negative exposure, the institution’s own default probability and its loss given default.

statement: If the credit spreads of both counterparties fall while the exposure profiles stay the same, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party are lower in magnitude.
explanation: CVA and DVA are each proportional to a credit spread times an exposure measure. With both spreads lower and exposures unchanged, every adjustment falls.
originalText: Because both spreads fell, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party will be lower in magnitude.

statement: If the credit spreads of both counterparties fall while the exposure profiles stay the same, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party are higher in magnitude.
explanation: Lower spreads mean lower default probabilities, so the adjustments shrink. Higher adjustments would require spreads to widen.
originalText: Because both spreads fell, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party will be higher in magnitude.
correction: If the credit spreads of both counterparties fall while the exposure profiles stay the same, the CVA and DVA recorded by each party are lower in magnitude.

statement: All else equal, a widening of a party's own credit spread reduces its DVA.
explanation: DVA rises when the party's own default probability rises, so a wider own spread increases its DVA.
originalText: All else equal, a widening of a party’s own credit spread reduces its DVA.
correction: All else equal, a widening of a party's own credit spread increases its DVA.

statement: CVA is the cost to a party arising from the possibility that its counterparty defaults.
explanation: CVA is the expected loss from counterparty default and is a cost to the party that is exposed.
originalText: CVA is the cost to a party arising from the possibility that its counterparty defaults.

statement: DVA is the benefit to a party arising from the possibility that it defaults itself.
explanation: DVA is the mirror image of the counterparty's CVA: the benefit of not paying in full if the party itself defaults.
originalText: DVA is the benefit to a party arising from the possibility that it defaults itself, and (with both parties using the same inputs) equals the counterparty’s CVA on the same position.

statement: Unilateral CVA reflects only the counterparty's default and unilateral DVA only the institution's own default, whereas bilateral CVA reflects both defaults, with each default conditioned on the other party not having defaulted first.
explanation: The unilateral measures each ignore the other party's default. BCVA applies survival (first-to-default) adjustments, so it is not a simple sum of the two unilateral numbers.
originalText: UCVA reflects only the client’s default and UDVA only the bank’s own default; BCVA reflects both, with each default conditioned on the other party not having defaulted first, so its CVA and DVA components are smaller in magnitude than UCVA and UDVA.

statement: Unilateral CVA reflects the default of both parties, while unilateral DVA reflects only the counterparty's default.
explanation: Unilateral CVA captures only the counterparty's default and unilateral DVA only the institution's own default. Bilateral CVA is the measure that reflects both.
originalText: UCVA reflects default of both parties; UDVA reflects only the client’s default; BCVA is exactly UCVA plus UDVA.

statement: Unilateral CVA reflects only the institution's own default, and unilateral DVA reflects only the counterparty's default.
explanation: The roles are reversed: unilateral CVA is the charge for the counterparty's default, and unilateral DVA is the benefit from the institution's own default.
originalText: UCVA reflects only the bank’s own default and UDVA only the client’s default; BCVA reflects both defaults with first‑to‑default survival adjustments.
correction: Unilateral CVA reflects only the counterparty's default, and unilateral DVA reflects only the institution's own default.

changes.from: only the institution's own default, and unilateral DVA reflects only the counterparty's default
changes.to: only the counterparty's default, and unilateral DVA reflects only the institution's own default

statement: Bilateral CVA can be positive because the debt value adjustment (DVA) may exceed the CVA, whereas unilateral CVA can only be a cost.
explanation: BCVA contains both CVA (a cost) and DVA (a gain). With a much riskier own credit, DVA can dominate and BCVA turns positive, which cannot happen with unilateral CVA alone.
originalText: BCVA can be positive because the debt value adjustment (DVA) may exceed the CVA, whereas UCVA can only be a cost to the bank.

statement: Bilateral CVA is always more negative than unilateral CVA, because it adds the cost of the institution's own default to the cost of the counterparty's default.
explanation: DVA is a gain, not an additional cost, so BCVA is generally less negative than unilateral CVA and may even be positive.
originalText: BCVA is always more negative than UCVA, because it adds the cost of the bank’s own default to the cost of the client’s default.

statement: Unilateral CVA can turn positive when an institution's own credit risk is large, whereas bilateral CVA is always a cost.
explanation: It is the reverse: unilateral CVA can only be a cost, while bilateral CVA can be positive when the DVA term outweighs the CVA term.
originalText: UCVA can turn positive when the bank’s own credit risk is large, whereas BCVA is always a cost to the bank.

statement: Unilateral CVA and bilateral CVA are equal, because the institution's own default cannot affect the value of a trade in which the counterparty is the only party at risk.
explanation: In a bilateral setting both parties can default, and the institution's own default gives rise to DVA, so bilateral CVA differs from unilateral CVA.
originalText: UCVA and BCVA will be equal, because the bank’s own default cannot affect the value of a trade in which the client is the only party at risk.

statement: When pricing a new trade under a netting agreement, the CVA charge is the incremental CVA: the CVA of the netting set with the new trade minus the CVA of the netting set without it.
explanation: Netting makes CVA non-additive, so the new trade's cost is the change in netting-set CVA, which captures the offset against existing positions.
originalText: Compute the CVA of the netting set with and without the new trade, and charge the difference (incremental CVA), which reflects the netting benefit.

statement: When pricing a new trade under a netting agreement, its stand-alone CVA can simply be added to the existing netting-set CVA, since CVA is additive across trades.
explanation: Stand-alone CVA ignores netting and overstates the charge. With netting, CVA is not additive across trades.
originalText: Compute the new trade’s standalone CVA and add it to the existing netting‑set CVA, since CVA is additive across trades.

statement: When pricing a new trade under a netting agreement, the CVA of the existing netting set is sufficient, because the effect of the new trade is captured by the counterparty's credit spread.
explanation: A new trade changes the exposure of the whole netting set. The credit spread reflects the counterparty's default risk, not the trade-level change in exposure.
originalText: Compute the CVA of the existing netting set only, since the new trade’s effect is captured by the counterparty’s credit spread.

statement: Incremental CVA is the appropriate measure for charging the desk that has just executed a new trade with the change in netting-set CVA caused by that trade.
explanation: Incremental CVA measures the change in netting-set CVA caused by one specific change (new trade, unwind, restructuring), which is the amount to charge the originating desk or client.
originalText: Charging the desk that has just executed a new trade with the change in netting‑set CVA caused by that trade.

statement: Incremental CVA is the measure used to split the netting-set CVA at a given date into trade-level contributions that sum to the total.
explanation: That is marginal CVA, whose contributions add up to the total CVA. Incremental CVAs are tied to the sequence of execution.
originalText: Splitting the netting‑set CVA at a given date into trade‑level contributions that sum to the total, for accounting purposes.

statement: Incremental CVA is the most appropriate measure for pricing several trades executed simultaneously with the same counterparty.
explanation: Simultaneous trades are a use case for marginal CVA. Incremental CVA would depend arbitrarily on which of the simultaneous trades is treated as first.
originalText: Pricing several trades executed simultaneously with the counterparty as part of the same deal.

statement: Incremental CVA gives each trade's CVA contribution in a way that does not depend on the order in which trades were executed.
explanation: Order-independence is the defining feature of marginal CVA. Incremental CVA is explicitly order-dependent.
originalText: Analysing each trade’s CVA contribution in a way that does not depend on the order in which trades were executed.

statement: Marginal CVA is most appropriate for calculating trade-level CVA contributions at a given time.
explanation: Marginal CVA allocates the total netting-set CVA across trades so that the contributions add up to the total.
originalText: Calculating the trade‑level CVA contributions at a given time.

statement: Marginal CVA is the most appropriate measure for pricing new transactions.
explanation: New trades are priced with incremental CVA. The marginal CVA of existing trades changes when a trade is added.
originalText: Pricing new transactions.

statement: Marginal CVA is the most appropriate measure for pricing trades transacted at different times.
explanation: Trades done at different times are handled sequentially by incremental CVA, which reflects the timing of each trade. Marginal CVA is used for allocation and simultaneous trades.
originalText: Pricing trades transacted at different times.

statement: The incremental CVA of a new trade cannot be negative.
explanation: Incremental CVA, through the incremental EPE, can be negative when the new trade sufficiently offsets the existing netting set, so there is no floor at zero.
originalText: It must be greater than or equal to zero; it cannot be negative.
correction: The incremental CVA of a new trade can be negative.

statement: Incremental CVA depends on the order in which trades are executed.
explanation: Each trade is measured given the trades already in the netting set, so the order of execution changes its impact.
originalText: It depends on the order in which trades are executed.

statement: The incremental CVA of a new trade is less than or equal to its stand-alone CVA.
explanation: Netting can only reduce CVA, so the incremental CVA never exceeds the stand-alone CVA.
originalText: It is less than or equal to the stand‑alone CVA of the new trade.

statement: Incremental CVA is useful for measuring the impact of adding a trade to, or removing a trade from, an existing netting set.
explanation: Measuring the impact of new trades, unwinds and restructurings is the primary purpose of incremental CVA.
originalText: It is useful for the impact of adding (or removing) a trade to (from) the existing netting set.

statement: By definition, marginal CVA must be less than or equal to incremental CVA.
explanation: Marginal CVA is an order-independent allocation, so it can be above or below a given incremental CVA depending on execution order. No inequality holds by definition.
originalText: By definition, marginal CVA must be less than or equal to incremental CVA.

statement: Unlike incremental CVA, marginal CVA is additive: the sum of the marginal CVAs of the trades equals the total CVA.
explanation: Additivity, with contributions summing to the total CVA, is the defining feature of marginal CVA.
originalText: Unlike incremental CVA, marginal CVA is additive: the sum of marginal CVAs is the total CVA.

statement: Marginal CVA is more relevant than incremental CVA for apportioning CVA contributions fairly across existing trades or for assessing the CVA of more than one new trade.
explanation: Order-independence makes marginal CVA the fair allocation for existing and simultaneous trades.
originalText: Marginal CVA is more relevant (than incremental CVA) for apportioning CVA contributions fairly across existing trades or assessing the CVA of more than one new trade.

statement: Whereas it is difficult to price simultaneous trades with incremental CVA, marginal CVA is the appropriate way to calculate the trade-level CVA contributions of several trades at the same time.
explanation: Simultaneous trades are a stated use of marginal CVA, since it does not depend on which trade is treated as first.
originalText: Whereas it is difficult to price simultaneous trades with incremental CVA, marginal CVA is the appropriate way to calculate the trade‑level CVA contributions of several trades at the same time.

statement: Marginal CVA of a trade is lower if the trade is executed second than if it is executed first.
explanation: Marginal CVA is order-independent, so a trade's marginal CVA is the same whichever order the trades are executed in. Only incremental CVA changes with the order.
originalText: W \< V; trade 1 has a lower marginal CVA if executed second than if executed first.
correction: Marginal CVA of a trade is the same whether the trade is executed second or first.

changes.from: is lower if the trade is executed second than if it is executed first
changes.to: is the same whether the trade is executed second or first

statement: The incremental CVA of the first trade executed equals its stand-alone CVA.
explanation: The first trade has nothing in the netting set to net against, so its incremental CVA equals its stand-alone CVA.
originalText: S = 92,593; the incremental CVA of the trade executed first equals its stand‑alone CVA.

statement: When trades partly offset each other, a trade's incremental CVA is lower if it is executed after another trade than if it is executed first.
explanation: A later trade gains a netting benefit against the trades already in the netting set, while the first trade has none.
originalText: T \< S; trade 1 has a lower incremental CVA if executed second than if executed first.

statement: When trades partly offset each other, the total netted CVA is lower than the sum of the stand-alone CVAs.
explanation: Both allocation methods sum to the same netted total, which is below the stand-alone sum because of the netting benefit.
originalText: X \< 392,973 and Y \< 392,973; total CVA is lower than the sum of stand‑alone CVAs.

statement: A risk manager who wants to know which trades have the greatest impact on a counterparty's CVA would use marginal CVA, because it breaks netted CVA into trade-level contributions.
explanation: Marginal CVA uses each trade's marginal expected exposure to split the netting-set CVA into contributions that sum to the total.
originalText: marginal CVA because he could break down netted trades into trade‑level contributions.

statement: Incremental CVA breaks down netted CVA into trade-level contributions, so it is the measure to use to see which trades contribute most to a counterparty's CVA.
explanation: The trade-level breakdown is a property of marginal CVA. Incremental CVA measures the change in CVA from adding one specific trade.
originalText: incremental CVA because he could break down netted trades into trade‑level contributions.

statement: Marginal CVA measures the change in CVA once a new trade is priced, taking netting into account.
explanation: The change in CVA from adding a new trade describes incremental CVA. Marginal CVA allocates the existing netting-set CVA across trades.
originalText: marginal CVA because it accounts for the change in CVA once the new trade is priced, accounting for netting.

statement: If the correlation between the default of a reference entity and the default of the CDS protection seller increases, the value of the protection to the buyer decreases because of wrong-way risk.
explanation: A higher correlation raises the chance that the protection fails exactly when it is needed, so the expected payoff net of counterparty default, and the value of the protection, falls.
originalText: It decreases, because a default of A becomes more likely to coincide with a default of B (wrong‑way risk), lowering the expected recovery of the protection payment.

statement: If the correlation between the default of a reference entity and the default of the CDS protection seller increases, the value of the protection to the buyer increases because joint default is more likely and the protection is more likely to be needed.
explanation: Joint default means the protection fails when it is needed, so it does not add value. A higher correlation lowers the value of the protection.
originalText: It increases, because a higher chance of joint default means the protection is more likely to be needed.
correction: If the correlation between the default of a reference entity and the default of the CDS protection seller increases, the value of the protection to the buyer decreases because joint default is more likely and the protection is more likely to fail.

statement: The value of CDS protection to the buyer is unaffected by the correlation between the reference entity and the protection seller, because it depends only on the default probability of the reference entity.
explanation: This ignores the counterparty risk on the seller. The dependence between reference entity and seller changes the counterparty-risk-adjusted value of the protection.
originalText: It is unchanged, because the CDS value depends only on the default probability of the reference entity A.

statement: Wrong-way risk is the risk that the exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with the credit quality of that counterparty.
explanation: Wrong-way risk is any unfavourable dependence between exposure and counterparty credit quality, which increases overall counterparty risk and CVA.
originalText: Wrong‑way risk

statement: Concentration risk is the risk that the exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with the credit quality of that counterparty.
explanation: Concentration risk is excessive exposure to a single name, sector or region. The adverse dependence between exposure and credit quality is wrong-way risk.
originalText: Concentration risk

statement: Settlement risk is the risk that the exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with the credit quality of that counterparty.
explanation: Settlement risk is the risk that one leg of a transaction is delivered without the other being received. The adverse dependence between exposure and credit quality is wrong-way risk.
originalText: Settlement risk

statement: Credit migration risk is the risk that the exposure to a counterparty is adversely correlated with the credit quality of that counterparty.
explanation: Credit migration risk is the risk of a change in rating or credit quality, with no link to the size of exposure. The adverse dependence between exposure and credit quality is wrong-way risk.
originalText: Credit migration risk

statement: One challenge in quantifying wrong-way risk is that historical data is uninformative about it.
explanation: Wrong-way risk may not show up in historical time series or correlations (zero correlation does not imply independence), so history gives an incomplete or misleading picture.
originalText: Uninformative historical data

statement: Buying an over-the-counter put option on one bank's stock from another bank creates wrong-way risk, because the performance of the two banks is likely to be correlated and an increase in the value of the put most likely coincides with a deterioration in the seller's credit quality.
explanation: The put gains when the bank stock falls, which is when a correlated seller bank is most likely to be in trouble. Positive dependence between exposure and default probability is wrong-way risk.
originalText: The performance of GigaBank and Alamine Bank is likely to be correlated, and an increase in the value of the put will most likely coincide with a deterioration in the credit quality of Alamine Bank.

statement: Buying CDS protection on mortgage-backed securities from a monoline insurer whose guarantees are concentrated in the mortgage market is a contract with significant wrong-way risk.
explanation: Protection bought from a seller concentrated in the very risk it insures pays out exactly when the seller is least able to pay.
originalText: Buying CDS protection on mortgage‑backed securities from a monoline insurer whose guarantees are concentrated in the mortgage market.

statement: Strong credit linkage between the reference entity and the counterparty creates extreme wrong-way risk for the seller of CDS protection.
explanation: Strong linkage creates wrong-way risk for the protection buyer, whose claim grows as the seller weakens. A protection seller has no growing claim on the buyer, so it faces right-way rather than wrong-way risk.
originalText: Selling CDS protection to a counterparty on Oracle’s own sovereign, because the strong link between Oracle and the sovereign creates extreme WWR for the seller.

statement: Derivatives with a commodity producer that is hedging its output price create wrong-way risk because the producer owes money mainly when prices are high.
explanation: A hedging producer owes money when it is most profitable and least likely to default, so exposure and default probability move in opposite directions. That is right-way risk.
originalText: Derivatives with a commodity producer that is hedging its output price, because the producer owes money mainly when prices are high.
correction: Derivatives with a commodity producer that is hedging its output price create right-way risk because the producer owes money mainly when prices are high.

statement: Buying an equity call option from a bank on that same bank's own stock creates wrong-way risk.
explanation: A call gains value when the stock rises, when the bank's credit quality is likely improving, so exposure and default probability move in opposite directions. It is the put that carries wrong-way risk.
originalText: Equity call options bought from a bank on that same bank’s stock.

statement: A derivative with a mining company that hedges its copper price risk typically exhibits right-way risk, because the company owes money mainly when copper prices are high.
explanation: A hedging commodity producer owes money only when it is most profitable, so exposure is high when default risk is low.
originalText: A derivative with a mining company that hedges its copper price risk, so the company owes money mainly when copper prices are high.

statement: Buying CDS protection from a seller whose credit quality is strongly linked to that of the reference entity typically exhibits right-way risk.
explanation: Strong credit linkage between reference entity and seller produces wrong-way risk, because the protection is least reliable when it is most valuable.
originalText: Buying CDS protection from a seller whose credit quality is strongly linked to that of the reference entity.
correction: Buying CDS protection from a seller whose credit quality is strongly linked to that of the reference entity typically exhibits wrong-way risk.

statement: Buying an out-of-the-money put on one bank's stock from another bank typically exhibits right-way risk.
explanation: A put on a bank's stock bought from another bank is the textbook wrong-way risk example, since both banks are hit by the same shocks.
originalText: Buying an out‑of‑the‑money put on one bank’s stock from another bank.
correction: Buying an out-of-the-money put on one bank's stock from another bank typically exhibits wrong-way risk.

statement: An FX forward with a sovereign in which a firm pays the sovereign's local currency and receives dollars typically exhibits right-way risk.
explanation: Paying a sovereign's weak local currency leaves the firm with gains exactly when the sovereign's credit deteriorates, which is wrong-way risk.
originalText: An FX forward with a sovereign counterparty in which Vertex pays the sovereign’s local currency and receives dollars.
correction: An FX forward with a sovereign in which a firm pays the sovereign's local currency and receives dollars typically exhibits wrong-way risk.

statement: Buying CDS protection carries extreme wrong-way risk if the credit quality of the reference entity is strongly related to that of the protection seller.
explanation: Gains on protection bought from a seller that weakens when the reference entity does may not be collected when needed.
originalText: Credit default swaps where Concord buys protection, which carry extreme WWR if the reference entity’s credit quality is strongly related to that of the protection seller.

statement: Mortgage derivatives pose wrong-way risk during an economic boom, because a boom increases the likelihood of borrower defaults.
explanation: Mortgage-related wrong-way risk arises in recessions, with falling property prices and higher defaults, not in booms.
originalText: Mortgage derivatives during an economic boom, because a boom increases the likelihood of borrower defaults.

statement: Financial institutions have countercyclical default probabilities, which reduces wrong-way risk on CDS protection sold on them.
explanation: Defaults of financial institutions cluster in downturns, so their default probabilities are procyclical, not countercyclical.
originalText: Credit default swaps where Concord sells protection on other financial institutions, because financial institutions have countercyclical default probabilities, reducing WWR.

statement: To limit wrong-way risk on an over-the-counter equity put bought from a dealer bank, the buyer should choose a stock in an unrelated industry whose fortunes have little link to the dealer bank's credit quality.
explanation: Wrong-way risk is reduced by choosing underlyings whose value is not driven by the same factors as the counterparty's creditworthiness.
originalText: Buy a put on the stock of a company in an unrelated industry, whose fortunes have little link to the dealer bank’s credit quality.

statement: Buying a put on another large bank's stock from a dealer bank limits wrong-way risk.
explanation: Another bank shares the same macro shocks as the dealer bank, so this is the standard example of wrong-way risk.
originalText: Buy a put on the stock of another large bank from the dealer bank.

statement: Buying a put on a financial-sector index from a dealer bank limits wrong-way risk, since the index diversifies across many banks.
explanation: Diversification across banks does not remove the common financial-sector factor. The index still falls when the dealer weakens.
originalText: Buy a put on a financial‑sector index from the dealer bank, since the index diversifies across many banks.

statement: Buying a put on the dealer bank's own stock limits wrong-way risk if it is struck in the money rather than out of the money.
explanation: A put on the counterparty's own stock gives the strongest (specific) wrong-way risk, and being in the money does not remove the link.
originalText: Buy a put on the dealer bank’s own stock, struck in the money rather than out of the money.

statement: A forward currency contract whose mark-to-market gain is positively correlated with the counterparty's default probability is an example of wrong-way risk.
explanation: Wrong-way risk requires a positive exposure to the counterparty that rises as the counterparty's default probability rises.
originalText: Zapex has a position in a forward currency contract where its mark‑to‑market gain is positively correlated with the counterparty’s default probability.

statement: A firm that has written (sold) a call option to a counterparty in the same industry is exposed to wrong-way risk.
explanation: The seller of an option has an obligation, not an asset, so it has no meaningful credit exposure to the buyer.
originalText: Zapex has written (sold) a call option to a counterparty in the same industry.

statement: A firm that has written (sold) a credit default swap to a counterparty whose credit quality is positively correlated with the reference entity is exposed to wrong-way risk.
explanation: The seller owes payments under the CDS, so it has no growing claim on the buyer. Wrong-way risk concerns positive exposure to the counterparty.
originalText: Zapex has written (sold) a credit default swap to a counterparty whose credit quality is positively correlated with the reference entity.

statement: A long oil commodity swap with an oil producer, in which the holder pays a fixed oil price and receives the spot price, is more likely to exhibit right-way risk than wrong-way risk.
explanation: A hedging producer owes money only when oil prices are high, when its business is strong and default is least likely, so exposure and default probability move in opposite directions.
originalText: Acme is long an oil commodity swap with an oil producer: Acme pays a fixed oil price and receives the spot price of oil.

statement: A long call option exhibits right-way risk if the interaction between exposure and counterparty default probability produces an overall decline in counterparty risk.
explanation: Right-way risk is defined by an overall decline in counterparty risk from the interaction of exposure and default probability.
originalText: A long call option experiences RWR if the interaction between risk exposure and counterparty default probability produces an overall decline in counterparty risk.

statement: A long put option is subject to wrong-way risk if both exposure and counterparty default probability decrease.
explanation: Wrong-way risk on a long put requires exposure and default probability to rise together, not fall.
originalText: A long put option is subject to WWR if both risk exposure and counterparty default probability decrease.
correction: A long put option is subject to wrong-way risk if both exposure and counterparty default probability increase.

statement: The 2007-2009 credit crisis is an example of wrong-way risk for a party that had sold credit default swaps as protection against bond issuers' default.
explanation: The buyer of protection held the exposure to the failing monolines. The seller of protection owed the payments, so it was the buyer that faced wrong-way risk.
originalText: The 2007‑2009 credit crisis provides an example of WWR from the perspective of a long who had sold credit default swaps (CDSs) as protection against bond issuers’ default.
